passage:
For thirty-one years Ilse Halden wrote down, on a card each night the sky was clear, how bright she judged the star Mira Ceti to be. She had no photometer. Her method was the one taught to her at fourteen: find two nearby stars, one plainly brighter than the target and one plainly fainter, and place the target between them on a rough scale of tenths. A single card of hers is worth very little. An estimate made by eye can be off by a fifth of a magnitude, and Halden's own notes admit as much; she wrote, after a bad night in 1961, that she would "not defend any one of these figures for a moment."

What she would defend was the run. Professional observatories in her lifetime had instruments far better than her eye, but they had committees, weather over a single valley, and schedules that gave a variable star perhaps four nights a year. Halden gave Mira eight hundred nights. When her cards were plotted in 1978, the scatter was wide but the shape was unmistakable: a rise steeper than the fall, repeating every 332 days, with the peak brightness itself drifting slowly from cycle to cycle. Nothing in the professional record of that period showed the drift, because nothing in the professional record was continuous enough to show it.

Her successors have sometimes described the cards as a triumph of accuracy, which is the wrong word and does her a disservice. The cards are not accurate. They are dense. A hundred crude measurements spread evenly across a season will fix the date of a maximum more firmly than four fine ones taken whenever a telescope happened to be free, and the date of the maximum was the quantity that mattered. Halden understood this perfectly; it is her admirers who have not. When the observatory at Kell later built its programme of nightly monitoring, it did not copy her instruments, which were nothing. It copied her calendar.
prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with
choices: the limits of estimates made by eye, and the instruments that replaced them
the difficulty professional observatories had in scheduling time for variable stars
the value of one amateur's thirty-one-year record of Mira Ceti
the founding of a programme of nightly monitoring at the Kell observatory
correct_answer: the value of one amateur's thirty-one-year record of Mira Ceti
explanation: The passage introduces Halden's thirty-one years of cards, then argues about what made them worth having ("The cards are not accurate. They are dense"). The Kell programme and the observatories' schedules appear only in support of that argument, and her instruments are dismissed in a clause.

passage:
The dome at Ferris was not heated, and by two in the morning Nadia had stopped feeling the pencil. She was six hours into her first solo run, checking a list of eleven faint stars against a chart, when a twelfth appeared where the chart showed nothing: a clean point of light, steady, not far from the head of Draco.

She did the arithmetic she had been taught to do before anything else. She checked the date printed on the chart. She checked that she had the right chart. She swung the telescope away and brought it back, and the point was still there, in the same place among the same neighbours. Then, because Ferris had no telephone in the dome and the walk down to the house took four minutes, she stood with her hands inside her sleeves and let herself compose, silently and in some detail, the letter she would write in the morning.

It moved. Not quickly — she would not have called it moving if she had glanced away and back — but in the eleven minutes she stood there it drifted a measurable distance against the field, and a satellite in a high orbit is exactly what drifts like that. She wrote down the time, the direction of the drift, and the words "not a nova," and went down to the house and slept.

Her supervisor, reading the log at breakfast, was pleased in a way Nadia found hard to take. He did not say that she had been right. He said that she had been slow, and that being slow was the whole of it: anyone can see something, and what Ferris paid her for was the eleven minutes. Then he told her, and she thought at first that he meant to console her, that he had once wired a discovery to three observatories at one in the morning and spent the following week writing to each of them in turn. He had kept their replies. He said he took them out and read them whenever he was tempted.
prompt: What convinced Nadia that the point of light was not a nova?
choices: it shone steadily rather than flickering
it stood where her chart showed nothing
it shifted position over eleven minutes
it returned to the same place when she swung the telescope back
correct_answer: it shifted position over eleven minutes
explanation: "in the eleven minutes she stood there it drifted a measurable distance against the field, and a satellite in a high orbit is exactly what drifts like that." Its steadiness, its absence from the chart, and its holding position when she swung the telescope away and back are what made her think it might be a nova in the first place.

passage:
The recipe for Turkey red ran to more than a dozen operations and took the better part of two months. Cotton was steeped in a bath of sheep's dung and oil, dried in the sun, steeped again, treated with alum, and only then brought to the madder. Between these came rinsings, a bath of ox blood in some workshops, and long intervals during which the cloth was simply hung up and left alone. The dyers of Rouen and Glasgow who bought the process from workmen out of Adrianople in the eighteenth century copied all of it exactly, down to the number of days, because they could not tell which parts of it were doing the work.

They were right to be cautious, though not for the reason they gave. Their own explanation was that the sequence was a unity, and that to disturb any part of it was to lose the whole. In fact most of the steps could have gone. What the oil bath accomplished, as chemists established a century later, was to leave a fatty film on the fibre; the alum then fixed a metallic salt to that film, and the colouring matter of the madder bound to the salt. Three operations, in principle. The dung and the blood contributed nothing that clean water and a little chalk could not have supplied, and the sun-drying was a way of getting the oil to stay put that a warmer room would have managed as well.

But no dyer in 1760 could have known which three mattered, and the cost of finding out was not evenly shared. A failed batch was not a bad colour. It was a cloth that looked right coming out of the vat and then walked away in the first wash, which the dyer heard about six months later from an angry merchant. Under those conditions, copying everything is not superstition. It is the cheapest insurance available, and it stays the cheapest until somebody can alter one step and see the result the same week.
prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with
choices: the chemistry by which madder is fixed to cotton fibre
why dyers reproduced steps that were not in fact necessary
the spread of a dyeing process from Adrianople into western Europe
the harm done to a trade by the secrecy of its workmen
correct_answer: why dyers reproduced steps that were not in fact necessary
explanation: The chemistry is introduced in order to establish that most of the operations were idle, and the passage then spends its last paragraph explaining why copying them anyway was the sensible course. Secrecy is never raised: the workmen sold the process.

passage:
When indigo from Asia reached the European market in quantity around 1600, the woad growers of Thuringia and Languedoc answered with a campaign of remarkable vigour. Indigo was denounced to town councils as a corrosive drug that ate the cloth it coloured; in several German states its use was forbidden outright, and dyers were made to swear an annual oath that they had used none of it. Historians long treated this as a plain case of an established trade turning the law against a cheaper rival, and in the main that is what it was. Woad was grown at home by a great many people and taxed accordingly. Indigo arrived in a ship.

The complaint was not, however, empty. The early consignments were adulterated: with sand, with ash, and in some lots with sulphuric acid used to hurry the dissolving of the pigment, which does attack cellulose. A dyer working from a recipe written for woad, and handling indigo as though it were simply a stronger version of the same thing, could indeed ruin a piece of cloth, and did. What the woad growers described as a property of the dye was in fact a property of the trade in it: unstandardised material sold to men who had not been taught to test it.

The distinction mattered, because the two accounts pointed to different remedies. If indigo were corrosive, the remedy was prohibition. If the trouble lay in adulteration and inexperience, the remedy was inspection of the imported cakes and a new set of instructions for the vat, which is, in the event, what came about. By 1690 the prohibitions were dead letters nearly everywhere, and the guild ordinances that replaced them read like assay regulations. The woad growers lost. They did not lose before they had obliged their opponents to state precisely what they were selling.

what was true in the woad growers' complaint against indigo

correct_answer: what was true in the woad growers' complaint against indigo
explanation: The passage grants that the woad growers acted from interest ("in the main that is what it was"), then devotes its second and third paragraphs to the part of their complaint that was true and to what followed from separating the two.

passage:
The fisheries officer's objection to the beaver was, in outline, thirty years old: the dams warm the water, and the trout of the Ashe cannot spawn in warm water. He had figures. Above the first dam the July temperature ran at 12.8 degrees; in the pond behind it, 17.4; and trout eggs laid at 17 degrees mostly do not hatch. The county had paid for the removal of nine dams on that argument, and the meeting at Ellerby was called to decide whether to pay for more.

Wren, who had spent two summers with a string of loggers in the channel, did not dispute the figures. She disputed what they were figures of. Her instruments sat on the bed of the stream rather than at the surface, and they found the pond stratified: a warm skin some forty centimetres deep lying over water that held at 13.1, fed from below by springs the pond had never covered before it was dammed. The trout, she said, were not obliged to live in the skin, and her tagged fish had not.

That was not the whole of her case, and she was careful to say so. Below the dams the picture reversed. The ponds released cool water through August into reaches that had run at 19 degrees before the beaver came, and it was in those lower reaches, not above the dams, that the year's redds were counted. A dam taken out in September would need a month to make any difference to the water above it, and would raise the temperature of two kilometres of river below it the following summer.

The meeting did not go her way. What it did was stop paying for removals until somebody had put loggers under the ice as well, since neither party could say what the ponds did in winter, and the officer's figures, whatever else they showed, had all been taken in July. Wren, who had brought two winters' worth of instruments in the back of her car, said that she would set them herself.

correct_answer: recorded temperature at the bed rather than at the surface
explanation: "Her instruments sat on the bed of the stream rather than at the surface." The meeting ends by asking for loggers under the ice precisely because nobody had left instruments out through the winter.

passage:
The Ellery Free Library opened in a converted chapel in 1871 with 2,140 volumes and a set of rules that told the reader plainly what he was there for. The founding trustees — three mill owners, a curate, and the borough surveyor — had raised the money on the argument that a workman with a book in the evening was a workman not otherwise occupied, and their first purchase list runs to history, travel, biography, the natural sciences, and eighty-one volumes of sermons. Fiction was admitted, after debate, to the extent of one shelf.

The borrowing ledgers survive, and they are less obliging. In the first full year, 61 per cent of loans came off that one shelf. The sermons went out eleven times in twelve months, four of those to the curate. By 1874 the librarian, a former schoolmaster named Isabella Frayne, was writing to the trustees that she could not keep the novels on the shelves, and asking for money to buy more of them.

What is interesting is the trustees' reply, which has been read as a surrender and was nothing of the kind. They granted the money. They also required that the fiction be catalogued by author instead of shelved as a single class, and that the annual report give the figure for total loans without breaking it out by category. The first of these made the novels harder to tally and easier to find; the second made the number nobody wished to publish impossible to extract. The trustees had not changed their minds about what a library was for. They had decided that the argument was better won quietly than lost in public, and Frayne, who wanted her readers and did not much care what was said about them, was content to let them have it both ways. The library's own centenary pamphlet, printed in 1971, quotes the first purchase list at length and the borrowing ledgers not at all.
